newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - British socialists see Labour win as step to revolution.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - British socialists see Labour win as step to revolution.

text.p: Walking into a dingy hall filled with red flags to hear talk of revolution and people addressing each other as "comrade", you realise Tony Blair has not persuaded all Britain's left-wingers to join him in "New Labour".
Blair's move to the centre ground of politics ensured Labour's victory in the May 1 general election but the passion of old-style socialists remains undimmed.
A meeting in central London just days after Labour ended 18 years in opposition shows there are some who see Blair's victory as only the beginning of a long march to power.
"Labour, despite its vote by the working class, is a bourgeois government and it rules for the bosses not for the workers," said Mark Harrison, editor of the Trotskyite newspaper "Workers' Power".
"The starting point for our whole position was that the working class dragged the middle class with them on May 1 and made an enormous difference to the political landscape."
"WHERE NEXT IN THE FIGHT FOR SOCIALISM?"

Around 80 comrades gathered for a post-election rally organised by Workers' Power in a meeting hall littered with Marxist texts and lined with posters demanding: "Where next in the fight for socialism?".

"Workers' Power" advised its readers to vote Labour, despite regarding Blair as something of a traitor to the working class roots of his party, which was founded at the start of the century to protect the rights of the workers.
But "Workers' Power" representatives argued that even a centrist Labour Party government would create a more fertile ground on which to spread their gospel of revolution.
"The recognition that Labour is different to the Tories is important, but it is the beginning of our wisdom and only the beginning," Harrison said.
"The Labour government creates a window now in terms of organising and mobilising the working class."

Blair has transformed the Labour party since taking over as leader in July 1994. Changes included distancing the party from the trade unions, abandoning its traditional tax-and-spend policies in favour of tight fiscal control and accepting the need for privatisation.
These moves have left some of Labour's grassroots supporters feeling abandoned and betrayed.

Speakers at the meeting included representatives of striking workers, trade unionists and members of various hard-left political groups such as the Socialist Labour Party (SLP) and the Socialist Workers' Party (SWP).
SOME ON LEFT HAVE LITTLE HOPE IN LABOUR

"I did vote Labour, but I can honestly tell you it's the longest time I've ever spent in a polling booth in my life," said Frank Carvery, a representative of 329 sacked dockworkers in Liverpool who have been striking for 20 months to get their jobs back.
These men and the 53 women on strike after losing their jobs at Hillingdon hospital in London, are typical of those who feel they have been forgotten by Labour.
They have few hopes that matters will change under the new Labour government, which they say sees them as an embarrassment and an awkward reminder of their socialist legacy.
"I don't think they are going to come along and save the day for us, I don't think they are going to get us reinstated," Carvery said.
Some speakers at the rally were more pragmatic, saying socialists should be encouraged by Labour's landslide victory, which provides a positive starting point to instigate moves to the left.

"The significance of Labour's victory is that we are closer to the revolutionary alternative we need," said one woman, a member of the SLP which broke away from the Labour party under the leadership of former miners' union boss Arthur Scargill.
"This time the rebellion is going to take place in a Britain that has moved leftwards."

The meeting reached a rousing finale as the comrades rose to their feet, clenched fists held high, to join in a verse of the Internationale, the communist anthem, as a "declaration of their continuing commitment to the struggle".
